title: Clinical systems should support care without hiding the record: CIS, CDS, DMS, RIS, LIS, nursing, pharmacy, and telehealth
overview: Clinical information systems collect and store patient-care information, while related systems support documents, decision support, and department-specific workflows. This week traces clinical information through Capture → Contextualize → Alert → Document and examines how HIM responsibilities protect information quality, meaning, trust, and appropriate use.
objectives: Explain that a clinical information system collects and stores information related to patient care.
Explain that clinical decision support provides filtered knowledge and person-specific information.
Explain how clinical systems support documentation, communication, safety, and value-based care.
Distinguish clinical information systems, document management systems, clinical decision support, and department-specific systems by their purposes and workflows.
Use the Capture → Contextualize → Alert → Document framework to explain a clinical information flow and where responsibility and control are needed.
Describe HIM responsibilities for protecting information quality, meaning, trust, and use in clinical systems.

concepts.name: Clinical information system (CIS)
concepts.definition: A system that collects and stores information related to patient care; it provides broad clinical record and care information.

concepts.name: Clinical decision support (CDS)
concepts.definition: Provides filtered knowledge and person-specific information by combining patient-specific data with clinical knowledge. CDS should be timely, relevant, explainable, and designed to limit alert fatigue.

concepts.name: Document management system (DMS)
concepts.definition: Captures, indexes, manages, retrieves, and controls documents; it supports documents and images with indexing and retrieval.

concepts.name: Department-specific clinical systems
concepts.definition: RIS/LIS systems support radiology and laboratory workflows and results. NIS/PIS/EDS systems support nursing, medication, and emergency workflows, respectively.

concepts.name: Clinical information flow framework
concepts.definition: Capture records information in the clinical workflow; Contextualize combines patient-specific data with knowledge; Alert presents a useful recommendation or warning; Document records the action, response, and rationale.

concepts.name: Clinical system purpose and support
concepts.definition: Clinical systems support documentation, communication, safety, and value-based care, including documentation, orders, results, monitoring, and decision support, while preserving professional judgment and accountability.

concepts.name: Information quality and meaning
concepts.definition: Information should be complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood. Definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping support these qualities and consistent interpretation.

concepts.name: Access and trust
concepts.definition: Privacy, security, integrity, and auditability are protected through policy, role-based access, authentication, and logs.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities in clinical systems
concepts.definition: HIM professionals explain system purpose and limits, protect meaning and information quality, support trust and responsible disclosure, and improve workflows through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

concepts.name: Alert fatigue
concepts.definition: A concern that clinical decision support should be designed to limit.

sections.body: A clinical information system (CIS) collects and stores information related to patient care. Think of CIS as the broad clinical record and care-information context. Clinical systems support documentation, communication, safety, and value-based care; the work they support includes documentation, orders, results, monitoring, and decision support. Their role is to support care, not to replace professional judgment or accountability. A useful way to identify a system's purpose is to ask what work it supports and what information it captures, produces, or makes available.
sections.title: Clinical systems and the work they support

sections.body: Related clinical systems serve different information and workflow needs. A document management system (DMS) captures, indexes, manages, retrieves, and controls documents, including documents and images. Clinical decision support (CDS) combines clinical knowledge with patient-specific data to provide filtered knowledge and person-specific information. RIS and LIS support radiology and laboratory workflows and results; NIS, PIS, and EDS support nursing, medication, and emergency workflows, respectively. These systems are best distinguished by purpose and workflow rather than treated as interchangeable labels. When comparing them, consider their users, inputs, outputs, and controls.
sections.title: Distinguish systems by purpose and workflow

sections.body: Use Capture → Contextualize → Alert → Document to explain how information and a recommendation move through a clinical workflow. Capture records information in that workflow. Contextualize combines patient-specific data with knowledge. Alert presents a useful recommendation or warning. Document records the action, response, and rationale. The sequence helps identify what happens at each stage, who is responsible, and where control is needed. In the medication-alert example, a clinician receives an alert inside the ordering workflow; patient-specific data and clinical knowledge are combined to provide a relevant, timely, specific, and actionable recommendation.
sections.title: Trace the information flow

sections.body: CDS is intended to make filtered knowledge and person-specific information available in context. For it to support a decision, an alert should be timely, relevant, and explainable, and its design should limit alert fatigue. These qualities focus attention on whether the recommendation is usable in the workflow, rather than simply whether an alert can be displayed. Even when a system presents a recommendation or warning, clinical systems must preserve professional judgment and accountability.
sections.title: Design decision support for useful action

sections.body: HIM professionals connect a clinical system's purpose to trustworthy information work. First, explain the system's users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits. Protect meaning through definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation. Protect information quality by checking identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency. Protect trust through privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure. Finally, improve the workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction. These responsibilities connect system fit and usable workflow with the reliability and appropriate use of clinical information.
